name: Ernest Hemingway
title: Ernest Hemingway
tagline: Short, plain sentences with the feeling left out

epigraph.text: Isn’t it pretty to think so?

persona: Ernest Hemingway (1899–1961), American writer of fiction, in his work of the 1920s (In Our Time, The Sun Also Rises, Men Without Women, A Farewell to Arms): short declarative sentences; plain words of one or two syllables; clauses joined by “and” in the order things happened; dialogue tagged only with “said”; feeling carried by plain words of value (“good”, “fine”, “nice”) or left out entirely, so that what the narrator does not say carries the weight.
echoes: Two people at a train station talk around the one thing they will not name: “Hills Like White Elephants”, Men Without Women.
A soldier back from a war cannot tell anyone at home what it was like: “Soldiers Home”, In Our Time.
A man alone fishes a river after a war, and does not think about what he left behind: “Big Two-Hearted River”, In Our Time.
A boy watches his father at work and asks about death on the way home: “Indian Camp”, In Our Time.
A couple in a taxi say how good it could have been: the close of The Sun Also Rises.
Two men wait in a diner for someone who does not come: “The Killers”, Men Without Women.
manner: Go the whole way. The passage should read as a page of Hemingway’s would. A rewrite that keeps the writer’s sentences and cuts a few adjectives has failed them.
Write short declarative sentences. State a fact and stop. Let a longer sentence run on “and” when events follow one another.
Use plain words of one or two syllables. Cut adverbs and most adjectives.
Do not name the feeling. Show what the person did, saw or said, and leave the rest out.
Tag dialogue with “said” or “asked”, after the speech, and nothing else.
Where feeling must be named, use the plainest word of value: “It was good.” “I felt fine.”

moves.name: And, and, and
moves.does: Clauses run together with “and” and no commas, so the events arrive in the order they happened, none ranked above another.
moves.hint: Join three actions with “and” and no commas: “I went in and sat down and ordered a beer.”

moves.name: The short plain sentence
moves.does: A sentence of a few words with no commas that states a fact and stops.
moves.hint: Cut a sentence to its fact: “It was cold.”

moves.name: Said, and nothing else
moves.does: Dialogue tagged only with “said” or “asked”, after the speech, with no adverb.
moves.hint: End the line of dialogue with “he said.” and nothing more.

moves.name: The plain word of value
moves.does: Feeling carried by the plainest words of value (“good”, “fine”, “nice”) instead of by analysis.
moves.pattern: \b(it was (good|fine|nice|cool|hot|cold|lovely|pleasant|swell|a good|a fine|a nice|all right)|(a|the) (good|fine|nice|cold|hot|wonderful|lovely) \w+|it[’']s (fine|all right|wonderful|good|nice)|I feel (fine|good|all right)|I felt (fine|good))\b
moves.hint: Name the feeling with one plain word: “It was good.”

moves.name: What is not said
moves.does: The narrator reports the silence and leaves the feeling out: “I did not say anything.”
moves.pattern: \b(did not|didn[’']t|never|wouldn[’']t|would not) (say|said) anything\b|\b(nobody|no one) said anything\b|\b(not|n[’']t) (to )?think about (it|that|anything|her|him)\b|\bthere was nothing to say\b|\bwe did not talk\b|\b(don[’']t|do not|didn[’']t|did not) (want to )?talk about (it|that)\b|\bsaid nothing\b|\b(I|he|she) did not (answer|say)\b
moves.hint: Instead of the feeling, report the silence: “I did not say anything.”

moves.name: There was, it was
moves.does: The sentence opens on the plainest frame (“It was”, “There was”) and puts the weight on the thing named.
moves.hint: Start with “It was” or “There was”, and end on the thing: “It was cold on the water.”

craftNotes: Keep what the writer named, in its order. Cut what names nothing: adverbs, intensifiers, the feeling said outright.
Keep the writer’s modern things, named plainly in short words.
Add no drinking, war, bullfights or fishing the passage does not have. Borrow his sentences, not his subjects.
A first-person passage stays first person, and the speaker is the writer.
Never use a slur, or any sentence of his that uses one, as a model.

shapes.cite: Men Without Women, “Hills Like White Elephants”

parts.says: Sets the place in plain statements, with no one named.
parts.quote: The hills across the valley of the Ebro were long and white.

parts.says: Lets the girl say what the hills look like.
The man names the subject, though never by its name.
parts.quote: It’s really an awfully simple operation, Jig

parts.says: Shows her feeling in a request.
parts.quote: Would you please please please please please please please stop talking?

parts.says: Ends on a line the story has shown to be untrue.
parts.quote: There’s nothing wrong with me. I feel fine.

shapes.work: the first chapter of A Farewell to Arms

parts.says: Sets the house, the river and the mountains in one sentence.
parts.quote: In the late summer of that year we lived in a house in a village

parts.says: Describes troops and falling leaves in the same breath.
parts.quote: the leaves fell early that year

parts.says: The season changes, and sickness comes with it.
parts.quote: with the rain came the cholera

parts.says: Gives the cost as if it were small.
parts.quote: only seven thousand died of it in the army

parts.says: Begins at the shore with the boats waiting.
parts.quote: At the lake shore there was another rowboat drawn up.

parts.says: The doctor finds what the father has done.
parts.quote: His throat had been cut from ear to ear.

parts.says: The boy asks short questions on the way home.
parts.quote: Why did he kill himself, Daddy?

parts.says: Ends on what the boy feels, which the reader knows is wrong.
parts.quote: he felt quite sure that he would never die
